where the first hand of M has ὑπερπόλους [exceedingly many], from which the corrector first made ο ὑπερπόλλους [the exceedingly many], then ὑπερπώλους [exceedingly many horses], which passed into several copies, and the Byzantine scholiast accepted it in good faith, interpreting it as πολυΐππους [rich in horses]. Xenophon and Demosthenes said ὑπέρπολλα [exceedingly many things]; Hippocrates used the singular ὑπέρπολλος [exceedingly many].
killing with hunger those who are far too many,
where it is said of Helen, who had crossed the strait.
Of Epaphus, who was beyond the sea in Egypt. Pindar and Sophocles used this adjective.
and in longing, a phantom from beyond the sea will seem to rule the house,
the divine calf from beyond the sea, the avenger.
A verb not known elsewhere: the more common form is ὑπερίσταμαι [I stand over, protect].
where it is restored from the scholium as ὑπερτάτως [in the highest degree], i.e. above all.
O queen of the deep-girdled Persian women, highest of all.
revering great Zeus, and the highest god of hospitality,
to stretch over, hold out as a protection

so that neither a great man nor any of the young may surpass the great net of slavery.
Hesychius: ὑπερτελής [surpassing]: τὲρ τὸ τέλος ἀφικόμενος [having reached the end].
of a torch shining beyond the strait.
and surpassing, so as to cross the sea, the strength of the traveling torch.

Photius and Suidas: ὑπερτενές [stretched above]: ὑπερανέχον [rising above]. Hesychius: ὑπερτενῆ [stretched above]: ὑπερανατείνουσα [stretching up over], ὑψηλή [high], where the lemma should be changed to ὑπερτενής [stretched above] with Musurus, unless there were two glosses, the former ὑπερτενῆ [stretched above], whose interpretation has been lost, the latter ὑπερτενής [stretched above], whose interpretation survives. Moreover, ὑπερτενῆ [stretched above] is taken from a verse of Aeschylus (fr. 127 c.) in Bekker's Anecdota p. 153, 11. ἀθηρής [without awns?]: perhaps the unyielding (ἀτηρής [unyielding] in the codex), or the resisting. Aeschylus in Agamemnon (Memnon according to Wellauer): χαλκὸν ἀθέριτον ἀσπίδος ὑπερτενῆ [the unharvested bronze of the shield stretched above]. (ἀθέριστον ἀσπίδων [unharvested of shields] Blomfield in the Preface to Agamemnon p. X.) Or the bright, the one gathered because of brightness, or the one despising and holding no account because of hardness; or the sharp, from the awns. Hesychius, ἀθερής [without awns?]: iron, unyielding (ἀτηρής [unyielding] in the codex), when it reaps. Or fit for reaping, or gathered because of brightness, sharp, or of ears of corn.
